title: Farid's successor
hook: tradition says Nanak met Farid's spiritual heir at Pakpattan and gathered Farid's verses

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oankar, who came to test Nanak and stayed to listen. Your line was learning bows. Did you learn the meaning of one letter? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

A box of letters turns up in an attic after a grandparent dies. Nobody else knew they existed. Someone has to decide: keep them, copy them, or let them go out with the old furniture. Words get lost that way, one attic at a time. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a meeting where a set of old verses could have been lost, and weren't. It happens in a river town in the Punjab, at the shrine of a Sufi poet who had died long before. Today: Farid's successor.
screen: `A BOX OF LETTERS IN AN ATTIC.` → `KEEP THEM, OR LET THEM GO?` → `A SUFI SHRINE BY THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: We met Sheikh Farid back in year one: the Sufi of Pakpattan, whose couplets in the Granth are in Punjabi, the language of the fields. Today is about how his words traveled. Tradition says that on his journeys Guru Nanak came to Pakpattan and met the man then sitting in Farid's seat, his spiritual heir, a Sufi teacher in Farid's line. The janamsakhis picture two seekers talking, not a contest. They ask each other about God, about love, about how a person should live. And in the telling, the Sufi recites Farid's verses, and Nanak listens closely enough to carry them away. Tradition says that is how Farid's couplets came into the Guru's keeping, passed along the line of Gurus until they were written into the Granth. Historians discuss the details; the story is the one Sikhs tell. Here is one couplet, from Ang 1378, in plain paraphrase: Farid, if you are clever and fine of mind, don't write black marks against anyone else. Bow your head and look inside your own collar. Notice what that does. It turns the sharp mind around. The cleverness that would make a list of other people's faults is sent to look at its owner instead. And notice something else about the page. Among Farid's couplets in the Granth sit couplets by the Gurus themselves, answering him, adding a line, gently turning a thought. A Sufi and the Gurus, side by side on one page, in conversation. The verses weren't just stored. They were kept alive by being talked with.
screen: `FARID WROTE IN PUNJABI.` · `NANAK MEETS FARID'S HEIR.` · `LOOK INSIDE YOUR OWN COLLAR.` · `THE GURUS ANSWER FARID ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `THE VERSES KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse of Farid. Take today's couplet. Say it slowly to yourself: don't write black marks against anyone else; look inside your own collar. Then use the sit. Let one person you've been quietly keeping a list on come to mind. You don't need to excuse them. Just set the list down for two minutes, and turn and look at your own collar instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Farid's successor. The Sufi in Farid's seat at Pakpattan who, in the story, shared Farid's verses with Nanak, so they could be kept.
Your line: the verses kept. Today, copy out one line someone older gave you, a saying, a recipe, a joke, before it's lost. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 737 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KING OF THE ISLAND.`

howItsDone: Sheikh Farid's couplets are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are read and sung in gurdwaras like the rest of Gurbani, and Sikhs retell the sakhi of Nanak at Pakpattan as part of how those verses came to be kept.

fork.reveal: in the story, Nanak listened closely and carried Farid's verses with him; tradition says that is how they came into the Guru's keeping.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a short verse or couplet; Farid's verses in the Granth are saloks.

notes: Tradition names Farid's successor at Pakpattan as Sheikh Ibrahim (Sheikh Braham); left unnamed in the script. Confirm whether to name him.
The paraphrased salok ('if you are clever... look inside your own collar') is Farid salok 6, Ang 1378: confirm Ang and wording of the paraphrase.
Claim that saloks by the Gurus (Mahalla 1, 3, 5) appear among Farid's saloks, answering him: confirm.
The route of Farid's verses into the Granth via Nanak is presented as tradition with 'historians discuss the details'; confirm framing.
